title: SYNDACTYLY, TYPE III
alt_titles: SYNDACTYLY OF FINGERS IV AND V

intro.text: This entry describes type III syndactyly (SDTY3), syndactyly of the ring and little fingers, which has been reported both as an isolated autosomal dominant malformation and as part of oculodentodigital dysplasia (ODD); isolated type III syndactyly appears to map to the same region as ODD.

paragraphs.text: Type III syndactyly is syndactyly of the ring and little fingers (Johnston and Kirby, 1955). It can occur as an isolated malformation, often with brachymesophalangia of the fifth finger (De Smet et al., 1994), and is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait (McKiernan and McCann, 1993; De Smet et al., 1994). Type III syndactyly also occurs as part of oculodentodigital syndrome (Gladwin et al., 1997).

paragraphs.text: Opjordsmoen and Nyberg-Hansen (1980) reported a family from northern Norway in which 9 of 22 members across 3 generations had spastic paraplegia together with neurogenic bladder disturbance and syndactyly. The main complaint was the bladder disturbance, an incomplete supranuclear bladder paresis (uninhibited neurogenic bladder), which appeared early in the disease. The authors suggested that the family probably represented an unusual form of hereditary spastic paraplegia.

paragraphs.text: Schrander-Stumpel et al. (1993) described a newborn boy with complete cutaneous syndactyly of fingers 3 to 5 on the left hand and fingers 4 and 5 on the right hand. His mother and maternal grandmother had been born with the same hand malformation. The mother had a thin nose and small teeth, and the grandmother's teeth had been very small, with enamel hypoplasia. Both women had normal eyes.

paragraphs.text: McKiernan and McCann (1993) reported a large family with 14 members who had syndactyly of the ring and little fingers (type III syndactyly). The clinical features varied between affected members. Three affected members had surgery in the authors' unit, and the senior author had previously operated on a fourth elsewhere.

paragraphs.text: Schrander-Stumpel et al. (1993) concluded that inheritance was autosomal dominant in a family in which syndactyly was transmitted through 3 generations from maternal grandmother to mother to son. Pedigree analysis of a large family with 14 affected members by McKiernan and McCann (1993) confirmed autosomal dominant inheritance of type III syndactyly. De Smet et al. (1994) concluded that autosomal dominant inheritance was obvious in their cases of isolated ring-small finger syndactyly.

paragraphs.text: Gladwin et al. (1997) studied a large family with type III syndactyly and atypical facial features. paragraphs.text: Brueton et al. (1990) raised the question of whether type III syndactyly and oculodentodigital dysplasia are separate genetic entities or part of a single disease spectrum, on the basis of a family with type III syndactyly and an ODD-like facial appearance but no other characteristic ODD findings. Schrander-Stumpel et al. (1993) concluded that their 3-generation family showed variable expression of oculodentodigital dysplasia and proposed that type III syndactyly and oculodentodigital dysplasia form a clinical spectrum. Gladwin et al. (1997) noted that type III syndactyly occurs as part of oculodentodigital syndrome but has also been reported as an isolated entity.
